title: The Foundry Disconnect: Intel Nails the Transistor, But TSMC Holds the Keys to Yield and Scale. - 24/7 Wall St.
content:
Intel can now build a transistor that rivals anyone in the world, yet its foundry business is bleeding billions while TSMC signs hundreds of outside customers. The two latest earnings reports expose a gap that transistor specs alone cannot close. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC | INTC Price Prediction) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) have both reported, and together the results set out the foundry race clearly. Intel posted its strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years as Intel 18A scaled up. TSMC answered with a fast 2nm ramp and a 66.4% gross margin. Intel can now build the transistor. TSMC builds it at a scale nobody else matches. Intel’s revenue rose 25.4% to $16.13B. Xeon did most of the work, with Data Center and AI up 59%. The manufacturing story improved too. 18A output came in approximately 25% above target, and CFO David Zinsner said Intel Foundry “has driven down the cost of our primary Panther Lake SKU by roughly 50% year-to-date.” Look at who those wafers serve, though. External foundry revenue was only $293 million, and the division lost $2.1 billion. Most of the proof of 18A still comes from Intel’s own chips. TSMC’s quarter ran on outside customers. Revenue reached $46.72B, and high-performance computing made up 68% of sales. Chairman C.C. Wei said: “All the AI players are working with TSMC.” That expansion has to be powered, cooled, and connected by someone too, which is the whole point of our free report on seven AI infrastructure suppliers that aren’t chipmakers. Intel’s CEO, Lip-Bu Tan, pitched integration, calling Intel “the only company that can design, manufacture, and build the entire range of computing solutions.” He also said EMIB-T packaging has a growing backlog and that Intel already uses High NA EUV on Panther Lake. TSMC is taking its time with High NA and plans to start using it in 2030. TSMC answers with yield. It has 79% of wafer revenue at 7nm and below. On packaging at 5x reticle size, Wei said “I don’t believe that anybody can do that today except TSMC, and the yield is excellent.” Gross margin slid 1.3 percentage points sequentially as 2nm diluted it, a small cost of leading the transition. Intel’s next node, 14A, is the real credibility test. I will be watching whether outside customers sign up and whether foundry losses keep falling. INTC fell 30.98% over the past month, even after Barron’s linked a recent jump to Musk’s Terafab comments. For TSMC, keep an eye on Q4 guidance of $52.3B to $54.3B and on N2 capacity, which the company expects to more than double in 2027. I respect Intel’s execution, and Xeon demand looks real. Still, I’m being asked to pay about 63x forward earnings for a foundry whose customers are still mostly Intel itself. TSMC trades near 21x forward earnings, with paying customers and yield it has already shown. That gap in valuation and customer base is the clearest difference between the two foundries. Intel shares have shown large price swings as the turnaround plays out. A major external 14A customer win would be the clearest signal for Intel’s foundry case. title: Taiwan Semiconductor Wants In on SpaceX’s Terafab — but Only If It Runs the Fab - 24/7 Wall St.
content: TSMC's CEO confirmed talks with SpaceX over the massive Terafab chip plant, but drew a hard line that could blow up the deal before it starts. Elon Musk has a very different idea about who runs the place. Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE:TSM | TSM Price Prediction) confirmed on its October 15, 2026 third-quarter earnings call that it is in talks with SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) about the Terafab chip plant. CEO C.C. Wei also set one firm condition: TSMC has to operate the fab. Wei said TSMC is “talking to one of our customers who is trying to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific,” and is checking whether it could use that capacity. An analyst asked whether the facility would be TSMC-owned. Wei did not commit to an ownership structure: “We are still in discussion, let me say that. Either way it would be possible.” He was clear that a Texas plant “must be run by TSMC.” That puts him at odds with Elon Musk. Earlier this month, Musk confirmed on X that the two companies had talked, but he wrote “we will build and run the fab,” with TSMC at most subleasing part of the facility. “We work very hard to expand our capacity in the U.S. This is necessary because most of our large customers are in the U.S., and they request TSMC to increase the capacity,” Wei said, adding, “We sent the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation.” The numbers support his case. Third-quarter revenue reached $46.72B at a 66.4% gross margin. HPC revenue rose 22% quarter over quarter to 68% of revenue. Fourth-quarter guidance is $52.3B to $54.3B, and full-year revenue is expected to grow about 44%. Wei’s demand for operating control fits with what U.S. plants cost TSMC. Management said overseas fabs will reduce gross margin by about 2% for full-year 2026, and that hit could grow to 3%-4% over the next few years. Capex guidance remains at $60 billion to $64 billion. Wei also made clear TSMC wants every order it can get: “We have no intention to leave food on the table for others.” SpaceX’s need for chips is large and growing. In the second quarter, its AI segment revenue rose 247% to $2.56B, and $15.83B of its $18.37B in capex went into AI computing. On that call, Musk said, “Our understanding within NVIDIA is that we will receive a very small percentage of their GPUs next year.” All of that AI expansion still has to be powered, cooled, and networked by someone, and we rounded up seven suppliers riding that wave in a free report on the non-chip side of the AI boom. Earnings per share came in at $4.60, ahead of the $4.46 consensus. Even so, TSM shares fell 3.05% to $416.90 in morning trading and are down 11.71% over the past week. SPCX fell 3.61%. Wei said TSMC has “been prudent in our business planning going into 2027.” On Terafab, he promised more details later: “If we have any solid conclusion, we will share with you.” The open question is who would run the fab, and any deal will have to settle it.
